newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt aims to speed up privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Egypt aims to speed up privatisation.

text.p: Egypt was intent on building an investor-friendly, market-oriented economy, and was trying to speed up privatisation and reduce red tape, Public Enterprise Minister Atef Obeid said on Tuesday.

"We strongly believe private investment is the engine for growth," Obeid told a conference looking at Egypt as an emerging market. "We have been privatising...one company per week. We'll try to do more.
"Continuous deregulation is taking place with redrafting a law to fit with a market-oriented economy," he said. "A lot has to be done in the way of bypassing bureaucracy."
Egypt has pursued reforms in earnest since an economically-oriented cabinet was appointed in January 1996.
Minister of State for Economic Affairs Youssef Boutros-Ghali told Reuters foreign direct investment was expected to grow to $1.5 billion in 1997 from $800 to $900 million last year.
The government has said that it plans to sell some or most of its shares in 91 state companies by the middle of 1998.

Just this week, it said it would offer for sale to the public shares worth 1.5 billion pounds ($440 million) in the strategic sugar, aluminium and steel industries, and Boutros-Ghali said the government was in the process of deciding which state bank to privatise.

On Monday, the cabinet decided to increase the private sector role in the telecommunications sector by approving plans for private investors to take part in a mobile telephone company via a public offering, with the state taking about 30 percent.

"We opened the markets for private investment in utilities. We are inviting the private sector to invest in cellular phones," said Obeid. "In utilities...in 1997 we are encouraging the private sector to invest in parallel with the government."

"We are inviting the private sector to invest in energy, roads, ports, airports and cellular phones, and the rest are coming...but we are not ready yet for the privatisation of the existing telecommunications system."

Boutros-Ghali said that as the country's regulatory framework develops, "what we define as strategic because it plays an important role in the economy...becomes less strategic and we can exert the necesary controls and safeguards over these sectors without having direct productive control over them."
Obeid told Reuters a new investment law approved this month would be coupled with a unified corporate law soon.

Fouad Sultan, chairman and managing director of Al Ahly for Development and Investment and a former minister, said the new investment law fell short of expectations. There were still different rules for private and public sector, small enterprise companies, and inadequate incentives.
The new law provides for tax breaks of five to 20 years, aims to cut red tape involved in launching a business and allows the state to give land to investors for various projects.
These include land reclamation, hotels, cargo and silos projects, rental housing, brokerages and certain hospitals.
Independent economists and private investors however, spoke of the challenges of investing in a country bent on privatising but still tied to a commercial code more than 75 years old.

World Bank economist Marcelo Guigale said these included streamlining backlogged courts, overhauling tax administration, making training institutes market sensitive, and abolishing constraints on small enterprises.
